units.la: De circulo lacteo.
units.tr: On the Milky Way.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: DISPUTATIONEM Physicam instituturi, o-perae pretium facturi videmur, si de Galaxia, quaestione philosophica, philosophico inge-nio dignissima, disseruerimus.
units.tr: Setting out to conduct a physical disputation, we shall seem to be doing worthwhile work if we discuss the Galaxy, a philosophical question most worthy of philosophical talent.

units.la: 2. De quo etsi diversae sint physicorum sen-tentiae, ut, quod is sit, dictu difficile videatur, vero tamen quid maxime consonum, inquiremus.
units.tr: 2. Although the opinions of the natural philosophers about it are diverse, so that it seems hard to say what it is, we shall nevertheless inquire what agrees best with the truth.

units.la: 3. Circulus itaq; Lacteus, qui non est φανταστὸς [?] seu imaginarius, sed realis (graecè γαλαξίας à lacte, quod Graecis est γάλα) definitur pars coeli, constituta ex multis ijsq; paruis stellis ultro citroq; dispersis, & ex earundem frequentia lumine harum confuso dealbata.
units.tr: 3. The Milky Circle, which is not phantastic [φανταστὸς] or imaginary but real (in Greek galaxias [γαλαξίας], from milk, which in Greek is gala [γάλα]), is defined as a part of the heaven, made up of many small stars scattered here and there, and whitened by the confused light of these, arising from their crowding together.

units.la: 4. Non enim esse Meteoron, sequentibus rationibus defendimus.
units.tr: 4. That it is not a meteor we defend by the following reasons.

units.la: 5. Nullum meteoron est perpetuum. Circulus Lacteus est perpetuus. Ergo non est meteoron. Assumptionem probat experientia, quia semper eodem in loco, eadem figura & quantitate conspicitur semper cum geminis & Sagittario oritur & occidit, quod fieri non posset, si esset meteoron. Omne enim meteoron mutationem aliquam subit, & tandem consumitur. At circulus lacteus nunquam consumitur, ne quidem virtute Solis versantis in geminis & Sagittario. Ergo non est meteoron. Quod rursus probat experientia quotidiana, quia circulus lacteus nunquam visus est neq; diminui, neq; augeri, neq; interire. Sed magnitudine in prima creatione illi indita, nobis semper apparet. Ergo non est meteoron.
units.tr: 5. No meteor is perpetual. The Milky Way is perpetual. Therefore it is not a meteor. The assumption is proved by experience: it is always seen in the same place, with the same shape and size, and always rises and sets with the Twins and the Archer, which would not be possible if it were a meteor. For every meteor undergoes some change and is at last consumed. But the Milky Way is never consumed, not even by the power of the Sun moving through the Twins and the Archer. Therefore it is not a meteor. Daily experience proves this again, since the Milky Way has never been seen to diminish, increase or perish, but always appears to us with the magnitude given to it at the first creation. Therefore it is not a meteor.

units.la: 6. Quid? quod sereno coelo semper est conspicuus (nisi nubili aeris interstitium impediat) & orientalis hujus circu-li pars Ii[?] pars semper transit per primum gradum cancri, in quo sol constitutus Solstitiū æstivum efficit: & opposita circuli pars semper transit per primum gradum Capricorni, in quo Sol brumam constituit, semper etiam bifida cernitur, semperq; circa Cygni & thuribuli asterismos deficit, semper deniq; arcum Sagittarij dividit & geminorum pedes.
units.tr: 6. Moreover, in a clear sky it is always conspicuous (unless the interposition of cloudy air hinders it). Its eastern part always passes through the first degree of Cancer, where the sun, when placed there, makes the summer solstice; and the opposite part of the circle always passes through the first degree of Capricorn, where the sun establishes the winter solstice. It is also always seen double, always fails near the constellations of the Swan and the Censer, and finally always divides the bow of Sagittarius and the feet of the Twins.

units.la: 7. Quæ omnia meteororum naturæ non solùm sunt contraria, sed eandem etiam prorsus destruunt & corrumpunt.
units.tr: 7. All these things are not only contrary to the nature of meteors, but also utterly destroy and overthrow it.

units.la: 8. Ex his patet, Galaxiam esse lumen quarundam stellarum per se lucentium durabile, quod natura cœlestis perpetua, non materia Elementaris constituit,
units.tr: 8. From these things it is clear that the Galaxy is a lasting light of certain self-luminous stars, which the perpetual heavenly nature, not elemental matter, constitutes.

units.la: 9. Quæ cum ita sint, certò constare arbitror, Aristotelis & aliorum opinionem esse erroneam, in regione ignea Elementari conspicuam. Nulla enim exhalatio potest esse tam compacta, ut etiam ultra annos 5000. durare & constare possit, quod in circulo lacteo deprehensum est.
units.tr: 9. These things being so, I am sure that the opinion of Aristotle and others is mistaken, which places it in the fiery elemental region. For no exhalation can be so compact that it can last and endure even beyond five thousand years, which has been detected in the Milky Way.

units.la: 10. Etenim quemadmodum omnia meteora calore & virtute solis procreantur & in regiones aëris attolluntur: sic eadem virtute & calore Solis rursum corrumpuntur & evanescunt.
units.tr: 10. For just as all meteors are produced by the heat and power of the sun and are raised up into the regions of the air, so by the same power and heat of the Sun they are in turn corrupted and vanish.

units.la: Logicæ.
units.tr: Logic.

units.la: 1. Partes dialecticæ cum sanioribus Logicis facimus Inventionem & Judicium (Græcè τοπικὴν καὶ κριτικὴν.)
units.tr: 1. With the saner logicians we make the parts of dialectic Invention and Judgment (in Greek topikē [τοπικὴν] and kritikē [κριτικὴν]).

units.la: 2. Hanc & natura & doctrinæ ordine posteriorem, illam priorem dicimus.
units.tr: 2. We call the latter posterior both in nature and in the order of teaching, and the former prior.

units.la: 3. Notiora enim & Simplicia ut præcedant: ignotiora verò & composita sequantur, jubet τάξις διδασκαλικὴ. Topica autem est notior & simplicior ipso judicio, ergo præcedet.
units.tr: 3. The order of teaching requires that the better known and simpler come first, and the less known and more composite follow. Topics is better known and simpler than judgment itself, therefore it will come first.

units.la: 4. Assumptio probatur, quia argumenta primùm inveniri necessum est, antequam rationis judicio subjiciantur. Non enim potest aliquis judicare de re nondum inventa.
units.tr: 4. The assumption is proved because arguments must first be found before they are submitted to the judgment of reason. For no one can judge a matter not yet found.

units.la: 5. Inventio est prima dialecticæ pars de inveniendis ar-gumentis.
units.tr: 5. Invention is the first part of dialectic, concerning the finding of arguments.

units.la: 6. Argumentum autem hic non est tantum, definitore Cicerone, ratio rei dubiæ faciens fidem, sed etiam quod ad aliquid arguendum affectum est.
units.tr: 6. Here, however, an argument is not only, as Cicero defines it, a reason that makes a doubtful matter credible, but also whatever is fitted to prove something.

units.la: 7. Arguere igitur hic non tantum est convincere, confirmare aut refutare, verum etiam exponere, illustrare.
units.tr: 7. To argue here, therefore, is not only to convince, confirm or refute, but also to set forth and illustrate.

units.la: 8. Judicium est secunda pars Dialecticæ de argumentis inventis, disponendis ad bene judicandum.
units.tr: 8. Judgment is the second part of dialectic, concerning the arguments once found, arranged for judging well.

units.la: 9. Dispositionem hic proprie accipimus: judicium vero dicitur per metonymiam effecti, quia judicium ex dispositione oritur.
units.tr: 9. Here we take arrangement in its proper sense; judgment, however, is spoken of by metonymy of the effect, because judgment arises from arrangement.

units.la: Rhetoricæ.
units.tr: Rhetoric.

units.la: 1. Partes Rhetoricæ duæ sunt: Elocutio & pronunciatio.
units.tr: 1. There are two parts of rhetoric: elocution and delivery.

units.la: 2. Inventionem, dispositionem, & memoriam tanquam improprias Rhetoricæ partes reijcimus.
units.tr: 2. We reject invention, arrangement and memory as improper parts of rhetoric.

units.la: 3. Nec plures sunt tropi, quam qui à Talæo recensentur: videlicet Metonymia, Ironia, Synecdoche & Metaphora, reliqui, qui inter tropos annumerantur, vel ad unum horum pertinent, vel recte ex Rhetorica ad Dialecticam transferri debent, peculiare itaq; genus tropi non constituunt.
units.tr: 3. Nor are there more tropes than those listed by Talaeus, namely metonymy, irony, synecdoche and metaphor. The rest, which are counted among the tropes, either belong to one of these or ought rightly to be transferred from rhetoric to dialectic, and so they do not constitute a special kind of trope.

units.la: 4. Porro Elocutio spectatur in tropis & figuris.
units.tr: 4. Further, elocution is considered in tropes and figures.

units.la: 5. In illis verbum mutatur à nativa significatione in aliam.
units.tr: 5. In the former, the word is changed from its native meaning into another.

units.la: 6. In his orationis habitus à vulgata consuetudine mutatur.
units.tr: 6. In the latter, the form of speech is changed from common usage.

units.la: Astronomicæ.
units.tr: Astronomical theses.

units.la: 1. Syrius est stella primæ magnitudinis, in ore canis majo-ris calidus & naturæ Martiæ.
units.tr: 1. Sirius is a star of the first magnitude, hot and of Martial nature, in the mouth of the Greater Dog.

units.la: 2. Hic exortu suo, qui fit in nostro Hemisphærio ad 4. Cal. Aug. Solis calorem vehementer auget & intendit, adeò ut tellus quasi vratur, hominum corpora exiccentur, & ca-nes in rabiem agantur.
units.tr: 2. At its rising, which in our hemisphere occurs about the 4th day before the Calends of August, it greatly increases and intensifies the heat of the sun, so that the earth is as it were scorched, men's bodies are dried up, and dogs are driven to madness.

units.la: 3. Hinc planum est magnam esse efficacitatem stellarum in hæc inferiora.
units.tr: 3. From this it is plain that the stars have great efficacy upon these lower things.

units.la: Sphæricæ.
units.tr: Spherical theses.

units.la: 1. Stellæ in cœlo sunt vel fixæ vel Erraticæ.
units.tr: 1. The stars in the heavens are either fixed or wandering.

units.la: 2. Fixæ sunt vel in certa forma vel extra formam.
units.tr: 2. The fixed stars are either within a determined figure or outside a figure.

units.la: 3. In forma sunt 122. quæ in certas imagines sunt redactæ.
units.tr: 3. Within figures there are 122, which have been reduced to certain images.

units.la: 4. Extra formā sunt tum in circulo lacteo tum extra hunc.
units.tr: 4. Outside figures there are some both in the Milky Way and some outside it.

units.la: 5. Erraticæ sunt septem planetæ.
units.tr: 5. The wandering stars are the seven planets.

units.la: Ethicæ.
units.tr: Ethical theses.

units.la: 1. Cum omnium rerum extremus seu ultimus aliquis sit constituendus finis seu summum bonum, etiam aliquid in quo hominis natura acquiescat, constituendum esse duco.
units.tr: 1. Since some last or ultimate end, or highest good, must be set up for all things, I hold that there must also be something in which the nature of man may rest.

units.la: 2. Illud. a. est ex sententia omnium philosophorum, ad quod omnia referuntur.
units.tr: 2. That is, first of all, according to the opinion of all philosophers, the end to which all things are referred.

units.la: 3. Nisi enim in rebus humanis optimum ac perfectissi-mum finem instituerimus, ad quem omnes alii fines refe-rūtur, infinitus fieret in boni appetitione progressus, ideoq; omnium hominum studia, omnis ars, omnis doctrina, o-mnes deniq; actiones inutiles & irritæ fierent.
units.tr: 3. For unless we establish in human affairs a best and most perfect end, to which all other ends are referred, there would be an infinite progress in the pursuit of good, and therefore the studies of all men, every art, every science, and finally all actions would become useless and vain.

units.la: 4. Hominis autem finis extremus seu ultimus est agnitio & invocatio Dei.
units.tr: 4. The ultimate and last end of man, however, is the knowledge and invocation of God.

units.la: 5. Errant igitur Stoici, qui virtutem politicam summum bonum esse statuunt.
units.tr: 5. The Stoics therefore err, who maintain that political virtue is the highest good.

units.la: 6. Et impia defendere conantur Epicurei, qui voluptatem summum bonum hominis finem esse asserunt.
units.tr: 6. And the Epicureans, who assert that pleasure is the highest good and end of man, try to defend impious things.

units.la: Corollaria.
units.tr: Corollaries.

units.la: 1. An Dialectica sit philosophiæ pars.
units.tr: 1. Whether dialectic is a part of philosophy.

units.la: 2. An Rhetorica sit vituperanda.
units.tr: 2. Whether rhetoric is to be condemned.

units.la: 3. An anima sit mortalis.
units.tr: 3. Whether the soul is mortal.

units.la: 4. An defuncti post mortem obambulent.
units.tr: 4. Whether the dead wander about after death.

units.la: 5. An sepulturæ extra urbem sint habendæ, & an omnes homines sint sepeliendi. A.
units.tr: 5. Whether burial places are to be held outside the city, and whether all men are to be buried. A.

units.la: Justa Lex Regit Homines,
units.tr: A Just Law Governs Men,

units.la: Disputabuntur in Collegio philosophico hora & loco solitis.
units.tr: To be disputed in the philosophical college at the usual hour and place.

units.la: AD PHILOSOPHIAE CANDI-datum Johannem Langium familiarem suum.
units.tr: To Johannes Langius, candidate in philosophy, his friend.

units.la: FRIGIDUS, aëria, nix & velut imber ab axe Descendunt primo vere ineunte modo. Ultra[illegible, ~2 letters] remeant illuc, sine frugibus unquam Arida: sed reddunt, pinguia, rura, prius. Sic etiam ingenuâ tempus qui fallit in arte, Non labor, absq; huius fruge peractus abit. Sed multos templis fructus parit, ante, scholisq; Et patriæ fidâ dexteritate præest. Artes ingenuæ siquidem sunt splendida dona, Aequore quæ nullo aut igne famève ruunt. Tela ergo è nitidâ, Langi, depromè pharetrâ, Inq[?]; hostes, forti pectore mitte tuos. Sic solus reliquis clarus, præ, victor abibis Contentus, viridi fronde tegente caput. Aureolam, æternâ, capies dum luce, coronam, Omnia, quæ viridi, secula fronde viget.
units.tr: Cold, airy snow and, as it were, rain fall from the sky when spring first begins. They return there again and never leave the fields barren of crops, but make them rich again, as before. So too the time spent on the liberal arts is never wasted labour, since its fruit is brought to the temples, to the schools, and to the country, where it serves with faithful skill. For the liberal arts are splendid gifts, which no sea, fire or rumour can overthrow. Therefore, Langius, draw your arrows from a bright quiver and send your shafts with a brave heart against your enemies. So you will depart alone, famous above the rest, a victor, content, with a green wreath covering your head. You will take a golden crown of eternal light, and all the ages that flourish with green leaves.

units.la: Quam dabit electis, sanctis pater optimus atq; Ultima, cum pandet clausa sepulchra, dies. Ergo vale applausu, Langi tu docte Joannes, Nominis atq; memor, secula (Comis) age.
units.tr: Which the best father will give to the elect and the saints on that last day, when he opens the closed tombs. Therefore farewell, with applause, you learned Johannes, Langius, mindful of your name, live (pleasantly) through the ages.

units.la: M. Georgius Molitor Marpurg.
units.tr: M. Georgius Molitor, Marburg.

units.tr: THE END.
